lines.text: From some of the oldest art on Earth to a hard-won democracy, through kingdoms, colonies, diamonds, gold and apartheid. This is the story of South Africa.
On the southern coast, in Blombos Cave, people engraved pieces of ochre about seventy-five thousand years ago, among the oldest art anyone has found.
Much later, farmers built the kingdom of Mapungubwe on the Limpopo River, famous today for a small rhino made of gold.
In the mid sixteen hundreds, Robben Island in Table Bay began its long life as a prison, a role it would keep for centuries.
In 1652 the Dutch founded a supply station below Table Mountain. It grew into Cape Town, the country's oldest city.
In the east, Shaka reorganised the Zulu army into disciplined regiments and built a powerful kingdom.
Meanwhile Britain had taken the Cape, and from 1835 Boer settlers trekked into the interior to escape British rule.
Diamonds were found at Kimberley, and miners dug the Big Hole by hand, making the fortunes of Cecil Rhodes and De Beers.
In 1879 Britain invaded Zululand. The Zulu won a stunning victory at Isandlwana, but lost the war, and their kingdom fell under British control.
In 1886 gold was struck on the Witwatersrand, and the city of Johannesburg sprang up almost overnight.
Two years later De Beers was formed, and it came to control most of the world's diamonds.
Britain and the Boer republics then went to war. Britain won after years of guerrilla fighting and camps that held many civilians.
In 1910 the colonies were joined as the Union of South Africa, a country ruled by its white minority.
Two years later, the African National Congress was founded to defend the rights of Black South Africans.
In 1918 Nelson Mandela was born in the Eastern Cape. He would become a lawyer, a prisoner, and the father of a new nation.
Kruger National Park was created from an older game reserve, a vast home for elephants, lions, leopards and rhinos.
Desmond Tutu was born. As an archbishop he would speak out fearlessly against apartheid and win the Nobel Peace Prize.
F. W. de Klerk was born, the man who would one day, as president, set Mandela free.
Jacob Zuma was born, a future president who would resign over corruption.
So was Thabo Mbeki, who would follow Mandela as president in 1999.
And Steve Biko, who would found the Black Consciousness Movement and die in police custody, to anger around the world.
In 1948 the National Party came to power and made apartheid law, a system of strict racial separation and white minority rule.
Cyril Ramaphosa was born. A union organiser, he would help negotiate apartheid's end, and later become president.
In 1960 at Sharpeville, police fired on people protesting the pass laws and killed dozens. The government then banned the main opposition parties.
At the Rivonia Trial, Mandela and other leaders were tried for sabotage. His speech from the dock became famous, and he was sent to prison for life.
In 1976 schoolchildren in Soweto marched against lessons in Afrikaans. Police opened fire, and the unrest spread across the country.
After his release in 1990 came years of talks, and in 1994 South Africans of every race voted together for the first time. Mandela became president.
A year later South Africa won the Rugby World Cup at home, and Mandela handed over the trophy wearing the team's jersey.
The Truth and Reconciliation Commission, chaired by Tutu, heard victims and perpetrators of the apartheid years, and could grant amnesty for full confession.
The caves near Johannesburg, rich in fossils of our earliest ancestors, became the Cradle of Humankind World Heritage site.
In 2010 South Africa hosted the first football World Cup in Africa, to the endless buzz of the vuvuzela.
And in 2024 the ANC lost its majority for the first time, and formed a government of national unity.
From ochre and gold to the ballot box, South Africa's story is one of long struggle and hard-won freedom.
